newsitem.title: UK: Major Zaire force unlikely, British sources say.
newsitem.headline: Major Zaire force unlikely, British sources say.

text.p: Britain believes it is unlikely that a large-scale multinational force will be needed in eastern Zaire because a reconnaissance mission found far fewer refugees in the area than expected, defence sources said.
The British aerial mission over eastern Zaire located only around 200,000 refugees and displaced people, compared with the 700,000 estimated by the United Nation's refugee agency.
The British figure agreed with a U.S. estimate published last week.
"We think it is unlikely there will be any requirement for a large multi-national force," said a defence source.

He said one of two British battalions readied to join the force to take aid to refugees displaced by fighting between Hutu rebels and the Zairean army was likely to be taken off emergency standby this weekend.

Contingents from more than 20 countries including Britain, the United States, France, Belgium and South Africa, were expected to join the Canadian-led force, now expected to comprise only 1,000 or 2,000 troops rather than the 10,000 originally planned.
The numbers were scaled down after refugees suddenly began pouring back into Rwanda last month.

But the U.N. said it believed there were still more than half a million refugees in the region, basing its estimate on people registering at refugee camps. Where the missing hundreds of thousands of people have gone is a mystery.
The British sources were doubtful of suggestions that they were hiding in the dense jungle, believing the reconnaissance missions would have spotted them.
The reconnaissance mission using a Canberra PR9 jet covered most of the areas of eastern Zaire where it was thought refugees would be found.

It spotted empty refugee camps and only handfuls of people on the move on the mud tracks that serve as main roads in the region. Only one large camp, of up to 150,000 refugees, in a valley to the west of Lake Kivu was identified.
This camp was in an area of cultivated agricultural land, suggesting the refugees were unlikely to be at risk of starvation, they added.
"We are not talking about Ethiopia here," said one source.
The sources also said nations involved in setting up the multi-national force were moving away from the idea of using airdrops to get aid to the refugees.

"We tend to regard airdrops as a last resort and the Canadians who were looking into it in more detail are beginning to think that way as well," said a source. "Enthusiasm for airdrops has faded in the last six days."
The alternative is to use ground troops to escort aid convoys.
The British reconnaissance mission based at Entebbe in Uganda faced a number of difficulties gathering its information.

The rainy season set in just as the mission began, leaving the area under cloud cover for large parts of the day, and two days ago a volcano erupted in eastern Zaire, spilling smoke and ash into the air and further obliterating the picture.
Bats posed another problem. Entebbe is at the centre of a bat migration route and for an hour each at dawn and dusk the air was filled with millions of the creatures.
